description: Team Neurosense is a team from Dhaka, Bangladesh, taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We built Forest Detective, a web app that uses NASA MODIS, POWER, FIRMS and GIBS data to explore environmental trends around any city and test whether the changes are statistically significant.
summary: **Forest Detective** is a web app that helps people see whether a city's forest is really shrinking and why. Users search any city in the world and load yearly tree cover from NASA's MODIS satellite data, climate from NASA POWER, fire detections from NASA FIRMS, and satellite imagery from NASA GIBS. The app runs statistical trend tests to show which variables are changing and whether the change is significant, forecasts tree cover to 2035, and tests whether loss lines up with hot or dry years. This addresses the Earth System Trend Detector challenge by turning raw satellite records into clear trend and cause analysis. It matters because the right response differs: planting suits climate-driven loss, while patrols and protection suit the rest. The results are associations from about 20 yearly points, not proof of cause, and the app says so.
details:
Forest Detective is a web app that lets anyone explore tree cover in any city in the world. The user searches for a city or clicks the map, and the app loads about 20 years of yearly tree-cover data for that area. It then runs three analyses:

  1. Trend Lab: scans every NASA climate and land variable for the selected place. It shows which variables are changing, by how much per decade, and whether the change is statistically significant. It uses two methods, an OLS regression t-test and the Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope, so the result doesn’t depend on one assumption.
  2. Forecast: predicts tree cover to 2035 with ridge regression, using year, temperature anomaly and rainfall anomaly as inputs. It shows an 80% range from a residual bootstrap and checks the model on the last three years of data.
  3. Cause analysis: asks whether tree loss lines up with hot or dry years, compared with what chance would produce. A circular-shift permutation test gives a p-value. If the loss does not match the climate, the app says that planting alone will not hold the forest.

Fire detections within about 25 km of the selected point are also shown from NASA FIRMS, and satellite imagery from NASA GIBS and Esri can be switched on.

Benefits

  • Local answers: most forest data is global or national. Forest Detective works at the level of one city, where decisions are made.
  • Clear next steps: the cause analysis separates loss that climate explains from loss that needs protection and patrols, so limited budgets go to the right action.
  • Works offline after first run: the city database is cached locally after its first download, and city search runs on that local copy.
  • Accessible controls: the intro video can be skipped with Esc or the Skip button, reduced-motion preferences show a still character, and mobile action buttons are provided.

Intended impact

The primary users are rangers, forest departments, and NGOs that need to choose between planting and protection. Students and teachers can also use the Trend Lab and case files to learn how trend tests and attribution work with real NASA data. The longer-term goal is to make satellite evidence part of routine forest management decisions. This impact depends on validation: the team plans to compare results with ground-truth surveys and to work with a local forestry partner before anyone relies on them for policy.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python 3.10+ with FastAPI and Uvicorn, HTTPX for data requests, NumPy for the forecasting and statistics, and the standard library for city data.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Leaflet map library, Esri World Imagery, and Google Fonts.
  • Data: NASA POWER, MODIS MOD44B tree cover (ORNL DAAC), NASA FIRMS, NASA GIBS, and GeoNames cities5000 (CC BY 4.0).
  • AI tools: Claude helped with the code. Gemini created the intro animation.
  • Hardware: Any standard laptop or desktop can run the app. It needs no GPU, and it needs internet access only for live data and the first city-list download.

How it is creative

  • Detective framing: each place can become a case file. The player examines evidence, such as temperature and rainfall patterns, and matches it to a likely cause. This turns a statistical result into a question people can reason about.
  • Ranger character: an animated ranger walks and digs on the map, and the quiz and points system make the tool feel like a game without losing its scientific content.
  • Navigation-style labels: city names are placed on the map like a navigation app, with smaller towns appearing as the user zooms in.

Factors the team considered

  • Honest limits: the results are shown as associations, not proof. The interface and the documentation both say that each result rests on about 20 yearly points and that the satellite pixels are 250 m across.
  • Reliable first use: the app warms up its city list in the background, and it explains the sound and autoplay rules so a presenter knows what to expect.
  • Clear setup: the README gives setup steps for Windows, macOS and Linux, and lists the tests to run.
  • Data care: the app keeps an API key in a local .env file, and it caches downloaded data so it doesn’t repeat requests.
